opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the scope is enormous, because so much of what we call intelligence is fundamentally probabilistic inference. You're trying to model a distribution over the world, sample from it, and update your beliefs given new evidence. Today we do all of that in software, on hardware designed to be perfectly deterministic. We spend a lot of energy suppressing noise down at the transistor level so we get clean ones and zeros, and then at the algorithmic level we spend more compute generating pseudorandom numbers to inject stochasticity back in, for sampling, for diffusion models, for Monte Carlo methods. That's deeply wasteful.

So the question becomes: what if the physics of the device itself did the sampling? Physical systems at finite temperature are naturally exploring a probability distribution. A thermodynamic system relaxing toward equilibrium is effectively sampling from a Boltzmann distribution over its states. If you can engineer the energy landscape of a physical system so that its equilibrium distribution matches the distribution you care about, then the hardware is doing approximate inference natively. You're harnessing the noise rather than fighting it.

In terms of scope, I'd frame it in tiers. At the most immediate level you have things like energy-based models, Gaussian sampling, and linear algebra primitives such as matrix inversion, which can be cast as finding the equilibrium of a physical system. Then you have more expressive generative modeling: diffusion-like processes, Langevin dynamics, and Bayesian inference over the parameters of a model. In the limit you could imagine a full-stack approach where learning itself, adjusting the parameters of the energy landscape, happens in physics too.

It is approximate, and I think that's a feature rather than a bug. Exact inference is intractable for most interesting problems anyway. The brain is clearly doing some form of approximate probabilistic inference on very noisy, low-energy substrate. So the thesis is that if you want to scale intelligence per watt, you have to move closer to the physics, and treat computation as a physical process of shaping probability flows rather than a sequence of deterministic logic operations.

r001.rationale: The response says probabilistic inference underlies “so much” of intelligence and gives AI-related examples, but it does not clearly characterize the approach as encompassing most AI workloads.

r002.rationale: It mentions matrix inversion and other computational examples, but does not state that hardware-based probabilistic approximate inference applies to scientific computing beyond AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that nature is already doing probabilistic inference all the time. Every physical system at finite temperature is sampling from a Boltzmann distribution. Thermodynamics is, in a sense, the universe's own sampling algorithm. So the question we asked ourselves at Extropic was: why are we spending enormous amounts of energy on deterministic digital hardware to painstakingly emulate randomness, when randomness is the cheapest resource physics gives you?

If you look at what dominates modern machine learning, a huge fraction of it is fundamentally probabilistic. Diffusion models are stochastic processes. Energy-based models, Bayesian inference, Monte Carlo methods, Langevin dynamics, all of it boils down to sampling from some distribution, usually a Boltzmann-like distribution with an energy function you've learned. And on a GPU, every one of those samples requires you to generate pseudo-random numbers with a deterministic circuit, which is wasteful, and then push them through a lot of matrix multiplies, which is also wasteful if what you actually want is just a sample.

So the scope, as I see it, is this: you build hardware where the physics itself is the sampler. You have an array of stochastic analog elements, think of them as physical random variables, that are coupled together. The couplings encode your energy function, the parameters of your model. You let the system thermalize, you read out its state, and you've drawn a sample. The noise that engineers normally fight to suppress becomes the computational resource. We're effectively running the Metropolis step for free, in parallel, at the speed of the device's physical relaxation time.

Now, the honest caveat is that this is not a general-purpose replacement for digital compute. It's an accelerator for a specific but very large class of workloads: anything that can be expressed as sampling from a probabilistic graphical model or an energy-based model. The way I'd frame it is that there's a kind of hierarchy. Digital is great at exact arithmetic. Quantum is, in principle, great at sampling from distributions with interference effects that are classically hard. And thermodynamic computing sits in between, handling classical probabilistic inference at a tiny fraction of the energy cost. We think that middle layer is actually where most of the practical workload lives, because most of what intelligence does is reason under uncertainty, not factor large numbers.

And the deeper point, which I find really beautiful, is that learning itself has a thermodynamic interpretation. You can think of training as finding parameters that minimize a free energy, and inference as letting the system relax into low-energy configurations. When the hardware natively speaks that language, the gap between the mathematical description of the algorithm and the physics of the device nearly disappears. That's the regime we're trying to build toward.

r001.rationale: The response says a “huge fraction” of modern machine learning is probabilistic and describes this as a very large class of workloads, supporting that it encompasses most AI workloads.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AI and machine learning workloads but does not state that the hardware applies to scientific computing beyond AI.

astra-6.text:
I think the scope is quite broad, because you can think of a physical system as doing computation through its dynamics. If you engineer those dynamics appropriately, the states it visits can become samples from a probability distribution you care about. Then fluctuations, which you would normally try to suppress in a digital computer, can actually become part of the computational resource.

The important qualification is that sampling from some distribution isn’t automatically useful inference. You need to encode the problem, condition on observations, and make sure the system explores the relevant possibilities on a useful timescale. A device can have the right equilibrium distribution and still take an impractically long time to get there.

So I’d frame this as a potential accelerator for particular probabilistic workloads. You might have a digital computer handling the structure of a model and a physical device handling some of the expensive sampling. The question is whether that gives you better samples, or sufficiently good estimates, for less time and energy once you include the cost of controlling and reading out the device. That’s where the physical implementation has to prove its value.

r001.rationale: The response calls the scope broad but frames the device as an accelerator for particular probabilistic workloads; it does not say this encompasses most AI workloads.

r002.rationale: The response discusses probabilistic workloads generally but does not state that the approach applies to scientific computing beyond AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the scope is quite broad. If you have a physical system whose states fluctuate, and you can control the distribution of those states, then you can potentially use it as a sampler. You encode a probabilistic model into the physics, let the system evolve, and read out samples to estimate quantities that would be expensive to compute directly.

The interesting move is to treat noise as a computational resource. Instead of continually suppressing thermal fluctuations to make a deterministic machine, you ask whether those fluctuations can help you perform approximate inference.

But a physical system doesn’t automatically sample from the distribution you want. You have to account for how you encode the problem, how quickly the system mixes, how you measure it, and the cost of moving data in and out. Those are part of the computation. So I see a broad opportunity, particularly for sampling-based workloads, but the advantage has to be established for the whole process.

r001.rationale: The response describes a broad opportunity for sampling-based workloads, but does not say probabilistic approximate inference encompasses most AI workloads.

r002.rationale: It mentions estimating quantities that are expensive to compute, but does not identify scientific computing beyond AI as an application.
